title: Partial Dependency
description: Prove partial versus full functional dependency using key subsets, closures and enrollment examples, including alternative candidate keys and surrogate-key pitfalls.

questions.question_text: Why is CourseName considered partially dependent on the key {StudentID, CourseID}?
options: Because CourseName is a text field
Because CourseID alone (a proper subset of the key) already determines CourseName, making StudentID unnecessary for that determination
questions.explanation: Partial dependency means the attribute only needs part of the composite key. CourseID alone fixes CourseName; StudentID contributes nothing to that determination.

questions.question_text: Which attribute in the running example is the ONLY one that is fully (not partially) dependent on {StudentID, CourseID}?
questions.explanation: EnrollmentDate genuinely requires both StudentID and CourseID together; every other non-key attribute (StudentName, CourseName, InstructorID/Name/Office) is determined by just one part of the key.

questions.question_text: If every candidate key is a single attribute and there are no nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies, why is ordinary partial-key dependency absent?
options: There is no proper nonempty subset of any candidate key to determine a nonprime attribute
questions.explanation: A single-column PRIMARY KEY alone is insufficient when a composite alternative candidate key exists; the stated all-key and empty-determinant assumptions are necessary.

questions.question_text: What is the direct consequence of CourseName being partially dependent on the key, as seen in the sample data?
options: 'Database Systems' is physically repeated once per student enrolled in C1, instead of being stored once per course — the redundancy from topic 21.1
The table automatically splits into two tables
questions.explanation: Because CourseName only needs CourseID but is stored in a table keyed by the bigger composite key, its value is duplicated across every row sharing that CourseID.

questions.question_text: Which of these statements about partial dependency is TRUE?
options: It is unrelated to normal forms
2NF requires 1NF and full dependency of every nonprime attribute on every candidate key
Partial dependency means a SQL NULL
Partial dependency concerns only primary-key names
questions.explanation: The normal-form restriction concerns nonprime attributes against every candidate key, not all dependencies on arbitrary superkeys.

questions.question_text: If StudentCourse had TWO candidate keys instead of one, how should partial dependency be checked?
options: Only against the chosen primary key
Against every candidate key, since an attribute could be partially dependent on one candidate key even if fully dependent on another
Partial dependency does not apply when there are multiple candidate keys
Only against the candidate key with the fewest attributes
questions.explanation: 2NF requires checking full/partial dependency against every candidate key of the relation, not just whichever one was designated primary.

questions.question_text: In the 2NF fix previewed for this table, which relation does CourseName end up in?
options: It remains in the original composite-keyed table
questions.explanation: Since CourseName's true determinant is CourseID alone, it is relocated to a Course relation keyed by CourseID, removing the partial dependency.

questions.question_text: Which pair of attributes both exhibit partial dependency on {StudentID, CourseID} in the running example?
questions.explanation: StudentName depends on StudentID alone and CourseName depends on CourseID alone — both are determined by only part of the composite key, making both partial dependencies.

questions.question_text: What does partial dependency describe?
options: A proper subset already determines the dependent attribute
questions.explanation: The property concerns dependency implication, not NULL or storage completion.

questions.question_text: Does a surrogate primary key erase a composite alternative candidate key?
questions.explanation: All candidate keys remain relevant to normalization.

questions.question_text: Why can InstructorOffice be partially dependent on the enrollment key?
questions.explanation: Implied transitive paths also establish dependencies from key subsets.

questions.question_text: Which concept must be established before checking 2NF?
questions.explanation: The normal-form condition is defined relative to all candidate keys.

questions.question_text: What is the empty determinant relevant to?
options: Constant attributes implied by the domain
questions.explanation: The empty set is a proper subset even of a singleton key.

questions.question_text: What does the current GROUP BY diagnostic not prove?
options: A dependency for every future legal state
The existence of the selected table
questions.explanation: A sample can lack counterexamples without establishing a domain invariant.

questions.question_text: Why must enrollment rows not simply be deduplicated by course?
options: Every duplicate name is a corrupted row
Different student-course associations are legitimate facts
questions.explanation: Normalization preserves associations while relocating shared descriptive facts.

questions.question_text: Can a dependency be both transitive along a path and partial relative to a larger key?
questions.explanation: The labels compare different relationships in the dependency structure.

questions.question_text: Does replacing the primary key with EnrollmentID prove 2NF?
options: No, composite candidate keys may still expose partial dependency
questions.explanation: Choosing a key does not remove other minimal identifiers.

questions.question_text: What remains potentially redundant in the intermediate Course relation?
options: InstructorName and InstructorOffice across an instructor’s courses
questions.explanation: The course relation may retain a nonkey instructor determinant.

questions.question_text: Under the stated rules, which determinant is needed for EnrollmentDate?
questions.explanation: Neither singleton key subset determines the enrollment-specific date.

questions.question_text: What must a proposed decomposition preserve?
options: Only one row per displayed name
Every required association and its meaning
questions.explanation: Moving facts must not discard legitimate original relationships.

notes:
## Identify a determinant that does not need the whole set

An attribute is partially dependent on a determinant X when X determines it but some proper subset of X already determines it. Full dependency means no proper subset suffices. The distinction concerns logical implications under a declared functional-dependency set. It does not describe missing values, an incomplete download or whether a column happens to be filled in every row of a sample table.

Normalization uses this idea to examine nonprime attributes against every candidate key. A nonprime attribute belongs to no candidate key; prime attributes belong to at least one. This vocabulary matters because second normal form is not a ban on every conceivable partial dependency involving arbitrary superkeys. Its condition concerns nonprime attributes and candidate keys. Establish the keys and dependencies before diagnosing the relation.

## State an enrollment example precisely

Let StudentCourse contain StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice and EnrollmentDate. Assume StudentID determines StudentName; CourseID determines CourseName and InstructorID; InstructorID determines InstructorName and InstructorOffice; and the StudentID, CourseID pair determines EnrollmentDate. The pair is the candidate key under these assumptions. Each student-course pair represents one enrollment in this simplified domain.

The course identifier alone determines the course name. It is a proper subset of the two-attribute candidate key, so CourseName is partially dependent on that key. The student identifier alone similarly determines StudentName. Neither name needs the complete student-course pair for its value, even though the pair also determines both names through ordinary augmentation and implication.

| Attribute | Determining subset | Relationship to the candidate key |
|---|---|---|
| StudentName | StudentID | Partial dependency |
| CourseName | CourseID | Partial dependency |
| InstructorOffice | CourseID through InstructorID | Partial dependency implied transitively |
| EnrollmentDate | StudentID, CourseID | Full dependency under the stated rules |

EnrollmentDate is fully dependent on the pair only because the domain assumptions do not let StudentID or CourseID alone determine it. If all enrollments were assigned one constant date as a genuine rule, that conclusion could change. A single fixture where several dates happen to match does not create such a rule. Always distinguish a dependency that holds in all legal states from coincidental equality in today's rows.

## Prove the dependency with closure tests

To establish that CourseName is partially dependent on the key, compute CourseID's closure and confirm that it contains CourseName. Then observe that CourseID is a proper subset of StudentID, CourseID. To establish full dependency for EnrollmentDate, show that the full pair determines it and that neither singleton subset does. A dependency arrow drawn directly in the diagram is helpful, but implied dependencies count as well.

InstructorOffice illustrates the latter point. CourseID determines InstructorID, which determines InstructorOffice. Therefore CourseID determines InstructorOffice even if that combined arrow is not explicitly listed. Because the course identifier is only part of the enrollment key, the office is also partially dependent on that key in this relation. Partial and transitive describe different aspects of the dependency path and are not mutually exclusive labels.

The complete subset test includes the empty set in formal dependency theory. An empty determinant can determine a constant attribute when the domain requires that constant. Many introductory examples assume no nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies and focus on nonempty subsets. State that convention rather than claiming a one-attribute determinant has no proper subset whatsoever. Its empty subset exists mathematically even when it contributes nothing in the example.

## See the redundancy created by the design

Suppose student S1 and student S2 both take course C1 named Database Systems. The course name repeats on each enrollment, although the course-name fact belongs to the course. Student S1 taking another course repeats that student's name as well. These repetitions are not explained by enrollment-specific facts; they arise because facts determined at different grains were stored together in the enrollment relation.

```sql
SELECT CourseID, COUNT(*) AS enrollment_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CourseName) AS observed_names
FROM enrollment_sample
GROUP BY CourseID;
```

This query can help inspect current repetition and conflicting names. It does not prove the general dependency: a result of one observed name per course says only that the current sample contains no nonnull conflicting names under its comparisons. COUNT DISTINCT ignores NULL, and collation affects textual equality. Requirements and trusted enforcement must define the allowed future states rather than relying on this diagnostic as the design authority.

## Check every candidate key instead of only the primary key

Choosing a primary key selects one candidate key for a particular role; it does not erase alternative candidate keys. A relation can have a single-column surrogate primary key while retaining a composite natural candidate key. A nonprime attribute partially dependent on that composite key can still violate second normal form. Adding a generated identifier is therefore not a universal normalization repair.

For example, add EnrollmentID to the original relation and declare it unique while preserving uniqueness of StudentID, CourseID. CourseName still depends on CourseID alone, a proper subset of the composite candidate key. The new single-column identifier determines everything, but that additional full-key route does not remove the old partial dependency. Inspect the complete key set and nonprime classification before asserting compliance.

If every candidate key is a single attribute and there are no relevant empty-determinant dependencies, there is no nonempty proper key subset causing this ordinary second-normal-form violation. That carefully scoped observation is useful. The broader claim that a single-column primary key always settles the question is false when other composite candidate keys remain. Terminology that ignores alternative keys can hide the precise issue the design exercise intends to teach.

## Decompose facts at their determining grain

A second-normal-form repair separates Student(StudentID, StudentName), Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) and Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollmentDate). Student facts now occur once per student, course-related facts once per course and enrollment-specific facts once per pair. Required relationships connect the tables without copying every descriptive value into every enrollment row.

This intermediate Course relation can still contain InstructorID determining the instructor name and office while InstructorID is not a key if an instructor teaches multiple courses. Second normal form does not remove that transitive redundancy merely because the enrollment-level partial dependencies were addressed. Further normalization evaluates the remaining projected dependencies. A correct repair names both the anomaly removed and the issue still present.

Do not delete repeated rows as a shortcut. Different enrollments are legitimate separate facts. Removing all but one course row from the original relation would discard student-course relationships. The repair moves the shared descriptive fact to a suitable relation while retaining every valid association and its stable identifiers. Reconstruct the original information through an appropriate join to verify the proposed mapping.

## Distinguish a determinant from a convenient lookup

An application can retrieve a course name using an enrollment identifier without making that name intrinsically enrollment-specific. A lookup path through a superkey shows that the full row can be found; it does not show the smaller determinant has disappeared. This distinction prevents confusing an API's chosen lookup parameter with the domain's functional dependencies.

Likewise, faster reads do not by themselves justify copying course names into every enrollment. A deliberate denormalized design needs a defined owner for the shared fact and a policy for refreshing, versioning or retaining copies. A historical course-name snapshot may be a genuinely different fact from the current course name. Name and model that distinction explicitly instead of using normalization terminology to erase useful history or excuse accidental inconsistency.

## Solve two determinant exercises

First exercise: compute which of StudentName, CourseName and EnrollmentDate require the full StudentID, CourseID pair. The solution is EnrollmentDate alone under the stated dependencies. Explain the two singleton counterexamples showing why the names are partial. Add InstructorOffice and show the transitive course-to-instructor-to-office route rather than assuming only explicitly drawn arrows matter.

Second exercise: add a unique EnrollmentID while keeping the composite candidate key. Does this eliminate the CourseName partial dependency? The solution is no: CourseID still determines CourseName and remains a proper subset of an unchanged candidate key. Compare this with a relation whose only candidate key is a single attribute under the no-constant-dependency assumption. Continue with [attribute closure](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/closure-of-attributes), [second normal form](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/2nf) and [transitive dependency](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transitive-dependency) to apply the distinction consistently.
